title: Model answers for Q3, Q6 and Q7: Into the Cloud and Letter from the Pass
subject: English Language
unit: Summer 2: Timed Sections A and C; mock
source: Written for english-language/y10 lesson 64 (Marked Section A practice (portal) and teacher-written model answers for Q3, Q6 and Q7 (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 64. Teacher-written model paragraphs. Compare them with your own, then redraft.

passage.title: Text One: Into the Cloud
paras: The path gave out an hour below the summit, and after that it was just rock and breath. I counted steps: twenty, then rest; twenty, then rest. My legs had stopped arguing and simply obeyed. At the top there was no flag, no view, only cloud, thick and white as wool. I laughed out loud. Six hours of climbing for a room with no windows. And yet, sitting there with a flask of sweet tea, I felt something I have never felt at the end of an easy day: I had earned the silence.

passage.title: Text Two: Letter from the Pass
paras: Dear Brother, I write from the inn at the foot of the pass, where we arrived last evening in a condition I shall not describe to our mother. The guide, a man of few words and fewer teeth, led us up at four o'clock by lantern. The ice was treacherous; twice I resolved to turn back, and twice my pride forbade it. We reached the col at noon. Below us the valley lay like a map unrolled, its villages no bigger than crumbs. I confess I wept, though I shall deny it if you repeat it.

passage.title: Model
paras: The writer makes the climb feel like a test of will. The rhythm of 'twenty, then rest; twenty, then rest' mimics the plodding steps, and the personified legs that 'stopped arguing and simply obeyed' show the body giving in to the mind. The anticlimax of the summit, 'no flag, no view, only cloud', is turned round by the final line, 'I had earned the silence', so the reward becomes inner rather than visible.

passage.title: Model
paras: The letter-writer uses understatement and humour to soften danger: arriving 'in a condition I shall not describe to our mother' hints at exhaustion without detail, while the guide 'of few words and fewer teeth' adds comedy. Danger is real ('the ice was treacherous'), and the balanced clauses 'twice I resolved to turn back, and twice my pride forbade it' show an inner struggle. The simile of the valley 'like a map unrolled' and the confession that he 'wept' reveal awe beneath the joking.

passage.title: Model
paras: Both writers present reaching the top as an emotional reward rather than a view, but whereas the modern climber laughs at a summit lost in cloud, the nineteenth-century traveller weeps at a valley spread 'like a map unrolled'. Both use first-person confession, yet the memoir's short, wry sentences ('Six hours of climbing for a room with no windows') contrast with the letter's long, formal periods, showing how each writer's time shapes the way feeling is admitted.
